The Trumpet manucode (Phonygammus keraudrenii) is a medium-sized passerine endemic to the lowland and hill forests of New Guinea and adjacent islands. As a member of the birds-of-paradise family (Paradisaeidae), it exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism in body size, a trait consistent with its polygynous mating system. Available data indicate that newly hatched chicks emerge weighing approximately 10.6 grams [Ww0 = approximately 10.6 grams], a value that represents the initial wet weight of the altricial nestling. The incubation period, estimated from comparative studies on the closely related short-tailed paradigalla (Paradigalla brevicauda), suggests that embryonic development proceeds over approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days] when eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This incubation duration of about 20 days [ab = about 20 days] aligns with the general pattern observed among paradisaeids of comparable eg at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]g size. The hatching event marks the transition from an albumen-buffered embryo to an exotrophic nestling that immediately depends on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and nutrition.

In contrast to the relatively brief developmental period within the egg, the nestling phase of the Trumpet manucode is notably protracted, as is typical for many tropical passerines that exhibit slow life-history strategies. Under the active metabolic conditions characteristic of this species, operating at a body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a predictable series of ontogenetic milestones have been documented. The young achieve fledging—marked by the development of flight feathers sufficient for sustained flight—at approximately 26 days after hatching [tx = approximately 26 days after hatching], a timing that is comparable to that of other similarly sized paradisaeids such as Paradiga at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]lla brevicauda. This phase of nest departure is followed by a period of continued parental care and dietary transition as the fledgling develops foraging competence. The relatively brief nestling period, in conjunction with the nestling's rapid mass gain, suggests a high rate of food delivery by the attending female.

Sexual maturation in this polygynous species occurs after a prolonged period of somatic growth. Reaching the stage of reproductive viability requires approximately 78 days after hatching [tp = approximately 78 days after hatching] when the individual is maintained at the typical adult body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This relatively early attainment of gonadal maturity at 78 days after hatching [tp = 78 days after hatching] is notable given the pronounced size difference between the sexes that subsequently emerges at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The interval between fledging and the onset of puberty is a period of intensive growth, during which the juvenile bird must acquire sufficient body condition to withstand the energetic demands of eventual courtship and display. In males, this process involves the development of the elongated, wire-like head plumes and the modification of the syrinx that produces the species' distinctive, resonant call. Females, meanwhile, undergo a similar but less morphologically dramatic transformation.

The transition to an active breeding life is delayed considerably beyond the point of physiological puberty. The time since birth at first brood represents a life-history decision point that balances continued somatic investment against the initiation of reproductive effort. Data indicate that female Trumpet manucodes typically defer their first successful reproductive attempt until approximately 730 days after hatching [tR = approximately 730 days after hatching] under the thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This two-year delay before first reproduction is characteristic of many birds-of-paradise and likely reflects the time required for young males to establish display territories or for females to acquire sufficient foraging experience to meet the energetic costs of egg production and incubation. During this extended pre-reproductive period, the individual achieves the full adult body mass that distinguishes the sexes, with females reaching an ultimate wet weight of 146.5 grams [Wwi = 146.5 grams] and males reaching 183 grams [Wwi = 183 grams], a size disparity linked to the demands of male–male competition.

The complete lifespan of the Trumpet manucode, measured as maximum recorded longevity under natural conditions, is estimated at approximately 20.5 years [am = approximately 20.5 years] for individuals experiencing the species' typical active body temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This considerable lifespan aligns with a slow pace-of-life syndrome common among tropical rainforest passerines, which combine extended longevity with relatively low annual fecundity. In terms of reproductive output, females typically lay a single egg per clutch, but the high frequency of nesting events compensates: available records indicate that a female produces approximately 1.5 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches per year], with each clutch containing a single egg [N_R_i = each clutch containing a single egg]. The basal metabolic rate supporting this extended lifespan and intermittent reproductive effort has been measured at 215.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 215.5 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when assessed at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], a value that is consistent with the resting metabolism of other comparably sized members of the Paradisaeidae and reflects the energetic demands of maintaining a large body mass in a humid, thermally stable environment.
